items.question: How do you think about the relationship between biology and LLMs in your research?
items.object: The relationship between biology and LLMs in biomedical NLP research
items.answer: I really got into this biomedical NLP direction of research, and I've been doing that for many years, using AI to facilitate biomedical research through NLP tools. In the past, it was just ontologies, knowledge bases like UMLS, and I've been kind of transitioning into how do we really use LLMs effectively in this biomedical NLP space? From all of this biology-accumulated knowledge, I started to become more and more passionate about how the brain works and how we can get inspiration from that to actually make LLMs better. So I think of my research as this two-way street between biology and LLMs.

items.question: How did your thinking about language models for specialized domains lead you to HippoRAG?
items.object: The research motivation behind HippoRAG
items.answer: At the beginning, before even starting, I was thinking about domain-specific LMs and how they're going to fit into the current NLP landscape. Really, because of the limited amount of data that there is in specific domains, it's kind of not a great idea to just pretrain from scratch in these limited-data domains. So I was more leaning towards, okay, RAG plus a very strong LLM trained on everything is probably your best bet. But in looking into that, I realized that RAG has some very major limitations. At the same time, my adviser and I were both thinking about neurobiological memory, in human long-term memory, and our ability to do continual learning, like we do continual learning in a way that is basically impossible for current LMs to do. So it was kind of this back and forth between these two ideas: there's issues with current models and current RAG, and how really to best utilize associative memory, the concept of associative memory in humans, to make this kind of synthesis of the two.

items.question: Why do you see knowledge consolidation as necessary for answering multihop knowledge-seeking questions?
items.object: Knowledge consolidation for answering multihop questions
items.answer: I think early this year I kind of realized the nugget of inspiration that made everything fall into place was this idea of knowledge consolidation through path-finding. Multihop questions, this idea that LLM chain of reasoning is not all you need for finding knowledge-seeking questions. Really, you need to have this preprocessing knowledge consolidation of your information in order to answer all the questions that you want. In the paper, we use this example of someone trying to find a Stanford professor that also works on the neuroscience of Alzheimer's. We basically show that if there's a bunch of a thousand Stanford professors and a thousand Alzheimer's researchers, if you just use path-following, kind of have an LLM look at your corpus, find the appropriate next step and then follow it, you would have to be looking at multiple thousands of documents in order to do this correctly. A human that just knows this professor is at Stanford and does Alzheimer's research will likely just remember this professor immediately.

items.question: How do you understand the hippocampal memory indexing theory that you based HippoRAG on?
items.object: Hippocampal memory indexing theory
items.answer: This is not perfect knowledge, right? This is just theoretical at this point. But the hippocampal memory indexing theory, which is what we based HippoRAG on, tries to explain a lot of empirical data on the hippocampus being important for long-term memory storage. In the mid-1900s, the patient H.M., who got their hippocampus resected, basically couldn't form new episodic or semantic memories, like long-term memory, and so people are trying to explain why the hippocampus is so important there. The hippocampal memory indexing theory basically posits that it's an index that just stores pointers to the actual memories in the neocortex, and it also stores associations between these pointers. It doesn't have any true information about what these pointers are; it just points them to the actual representations in whatever area of neocortex they should lie in, like visual cortex, motor cortex, your language areas, et cetera. The idea is that as you obtain new knowledge, you build this associative index iteratively. So in our Stanford professor example, you would create a representation for the Stanford professor, link it to Stanford.

items.question: How do you understand the distinction between pattern separation and pattern completion in hippocampal memory indexing theory?
items.object: Pattern separation and pattern completion in hippocampal memory indexing theory
items.answer:
The hippocampal memory indexing theory kind of posits that there's three major components of human long-term memory. There's the hippocampus, obviously, that kind of does this associative index, but there's also the neocortex that actually represents the memories that you want to retrieve or re-experience, and then there's the parahippocampal regions, like the entorhinal cortex and other areas that sit around the hippocampus. Theoretically, it seems that this area serves as a link between the hippocampus and the neocortex, like a bidirectional information channel, basically. There's some ideas that some part of working memory is done in the parahippocampal regions, but this is still not very clear.

These three components work together to create two fundamental characteristics of human long-term memory. There's pattern separation, which basically allows you to disentangle different features that you experience, create concepts like Stanford professor and Alzheimer's research, or any sort of feature disambiguation or separation. Then pattern completion, which allows you to join together things that were relevant to a particular experience in the relevant ways.

Pattern separation is done through the neocortex and the parahippocampal regions. Through the neocortex, it's mostly done, I believe—this is not explicitly said in the literature—as a part of the language system that separates concepts out. The parahippocampal region also has a lot of sparsity; it's very overparameterized, so it allows for this kind of separation of patterns and features that then map into the hippocampus. The hippocampus is mostly for the pattern completion part. Specifically, there's a subregion called CA3 that's hyperconnected, so there's a lot more associative connections than in other parts. You would have this recurrence nature that allows you to remember things that are only associated because of your prior experience, not because they're associated semantically.

items.question: How did you translate your understanding of human long-term memory into HippoRAG's design?
items.object: HippoRAG's translation of biological memory principles into retrieval architecture
items.answer:
Based on these two fundamental characteristics—pattern separation and pattern completion—and also on the three components of hippocampal memory, we built HippoRAG to mirror those things. The neocortex and the language abilities of the neocortex we modeled through a large language model, because it has these local reasoning abilities and the ability to extract and disentangle features from language. We used retrieval encoders for the bidirectional bridge between the neocortex and the hippocampus, and a knowledge graph to represent the actual structure of the hippocampus. We use personalized PageRank to model the associative memory component of the hippocampus. Those are the three components that make pattern separation and pattern completion possible.

To do pattern separation, we link it to the offline indexing process, which is the preprocessing that you have to do to turn the corpus you have into an associative index. We first pipe each document through the large language model to extract entities. That grounds the next step of generation, which is open information extraction, or schema-less knowledge base construction. This has no rigid constraints on the type of entities, relations, or even the entities themselves that you can generate. We use the named entity recognition of the first step to ground that second step, but it's just a bias, not a forced constraint. It generates a lot of different entities and relations. We build the knowledge graph based on those triples extracted, and then use the retrieval encoders to build synonymy edges. This is a detail of the implementation that is quite important in specific cases: you need some sort of disambiguation, or actually synonym detection, the opposite of disambiguation, for this knowledge base to be more connected.

The online retrieval, which we linked to pattern completion, also has a pattern separation part, which is the named entity recognition from your question. Whenever a question enters and you already have your knowledge graph constructed, you first extract the features you want to attend to, then link them to the knowledge graph via the retrieval encoders, so you find the nodes that are most relevant. With those entities, you begin your personalized PageRank algorithm, which does random walks around your relevant entities until you converge on a distribution of probability. That gives you a distribution of probability over the nodes in your graph, which informs your ranking for your corpus.

items.question: How do you understand the parahippocampal region's role in transforming rich brain representations into memories?
items.object: The parahippocampal region's role in creating sparse memory representations
items.answer: I think, as I see it, it's kind of a sparsity constraint on the dense representations. The role of the neocortex is to experience the world and predict the world in real time, so the representations have to be really dense and rich. But in order to remember them, you need sparsity. I think the parahippocampal region is kind of doing this sparsity constraint. I'm actually not super sure about whether the sparsity is polysemantic like the large language model sparsity, because in the hippocampus we know there are several studies that find such things as place cells, people cells, grandmother neurons, different sorts of very specific, monosemantic concepts that we care about that are encoded in the hippocampus. Somehow it went from this dense representation in the brain that has all sorts of polysemantic stuff in a high-dimensional vector space, and then it gets sparsified in ways that we maybe care about, stored in the hippocampus. In that parahippocampal region, you are doing a lot of pattern separation, a lot of specification, in order to get to this level. I think there is a lot that goes on in the parahippocampal region that is not fully understood, and it's definitely not exactly like HippoRAG in any way. This is just a good implementation that works well, hopefully, at this point.

items.question: Why did you choose GPT-3.5 for HippoRAG's offline information extraction?
items.object: GPT-3.5 for HippoRAG's offline information extraction
items.answer:
GPT-3.5 is much cheaper than other models. The difference between 3.5 and Claude is that Claude is twice as expensive on the inputs and ten times as expensive on the outputs. That puts a constraint on our methodology because offline indexing is somewhat expensive, so you have to produce a lot of open IE triples. If you were to do our same experiments using Claude or GPT-4, you would have to spend around $500 to do the small subset of the three benchmarks that we did. That's a very limited subset: we use 1,000 questions and around 10,000 documents per benchmark. That would just cost too much money.

Honestly, the biggest reason I used 3.5 is that the task itself is not really a reasoning task, it's an extraction task. It's salience detection, and when two entities appear in a sentence together they have some relation, so detect the relation. It's kind of simple, and different LLMs—even Llama 7 billion—are able to do a fairly good job at this task. Apart from the formatting, which is kind of challenging and you probably need to fine-tune, because it's just an extraction task it seems quite simple for less intelligent LMs to do. I wouldn't expect Claude or GPT-4o to do much better on this task just right off the bat.

items.question: How do you assess personalized PageRank as HippoRAG's graph traversal method?
items.object: Personalized PageRank as HippoRAG's graph traversal method
items.answer:
This is kind of the biggest limitation of our framework, and the thing that we're most excited to work on, because PPR is obviously a very naive way to spider out from the relevant nodes. If a node is connected to your relevant nodes, directly and indirectly, it'll get more probability. The closer nodes get more probability, and if a node is connected to both relevant nodes it'll get more probability. So it's based on the connectivity structure of the graph, and there's no relation-guided anything like that. It's basically just how connected these nodes are to the relevant nodes.

If you turn up the number of steps that your random walk takes before converging, you'll just do PageRank on the whole graph. If you turn it up to the maximum number of steps, then you just get the nodes that are the most connected in your graph, the most popular nodes. That was used in the original Google Search: if your websites are very popular, just give me those instead of others. But that's not really a good idea here. If you turn it down too much, then the nodes you get are basically all you're going to attend to. There's a middle ground you want for the neighborhoods around the relevant nodes and between them in order to obtain good performance. I think our good performance in the benchmarks is due somewhat to biases and the lack of a lot of distractors, but if you make this a large-scale production corpus, you definitely need to make that graph traversal better. That's one of the things we're working on right now.

items.question: How do you assess the significance of HippoRAG’s benchmark results?
items.object: HippoRAG’s empirical performance and combination with iterative RAG
items.answer:
On average we compete with iterative retrieval, basically kind of head-to-head. We get a little bit better at some benchmarks and a little bit worse at others, but with a tenfold decrease in cost and time spent doing the online retrieval. That's huge for any production system that requires fast online access by your users. The indexing costs can be brought down a lot by using smaller LLMs, as I discussed earlier.

Another really interesting thing is that when you combine it with naive iterative RAG, you can get very large boosts on average, like 7 to 8% across benchmarks. That's basically proto-self-correction that you were discussing earlier, because the model is seeing the results of your ranking and it's able to reason better because you're able to do some associative memory retrieval. Those are generally the highlights of the empirical benchmarks that we showed.

items.object: HippoRAG’s potential for path-finding question answering
items.answer: Obviously, there's no empirical benchmark that exists that tests path-finding question answering, this Stanford professor/Alzheimer's researcher idea. This is something that you could not do with current approaches. We tried it on a few test cases, more qualitative, and it seems to do okay; it seems to do well on some of these questions. We need to make the graph traversal better in order to fully unlock its potential, but the idea is that you can try to answer all these path-finding questions, some of which are extremely important.

items.question: How do you assess the GAIA benchmark as an evaluation option for HippoRAG?
items.object: GAIA benchmark as an evaluation option for HippoRAG
items.answer: I'm familiar with this benchmark. It's very related, and I think we explored it as an option for this. The web-browsing portion of this is similar. However, because there's no standard corpus, it makes it a little bit challenging to do preprocessing. The whole internet is obviously still a challenge for our highest scale, or more like a cost. I think it's too costly to index all of the internet. Something like GAIA, but just maybe more constrained, would be a good benchmark for a setting.

items.object: HippoRAG’s distinction between path-following and path-finding
items.answer: I don't think the distinction between path-following and path-finding is very crisp in the current literature. I think that's honestly one of the coolest theoretical, idea-based things that Hippo does: it specifically defines this distinction. Both of those GAIA questions seem very hard, but they're actually just path-following questions, because there's a bunch of details about what type of fish you're talking about, right? The complexity of the question increases due to the number of hops, not really because of the nature of the task. items.question: How do you understand the limitations of HippoRAG’s entity-centric approach to graph traversal?
items.object: HippoRAG’s entity-centric graph traversal and the concept-versus-context tradeoff
items.answer: Graph traversal is one of these directions where I think we need to improve it ASAP. I talked about it in the paper as well: the concept-versus-context tradeoff. The entity-centric nature of Hippo allows it to do a lot of these multihop question-answering tasks and do well on these benchmarks, but it's not necessarily super generalizable. If you look at the examples I used in the paper, there's one where a question requires an entity to answer it, and this is a great approach. But there's a question in MuSiQue about the person that discovered there's a unique number of protons in every element. That doesn't have a named entity, and so the model kind of hallucinates proton as a named entity or as an entity of some sort. If you start from there in the graph, you'll completely screw up the results. This query requires a lot of context and contextualization of the entities in the query. We're working on finding a better way to map from the query to entry points in the graph. A lot of people have worked on this in the past, so we're playing around with things people have done. I don't think it's extremely difficult, but it's definitely a very obvious improvement that Hippo will have to go through.

items.question: How would you combine standard RAG's semantic document retrieval with HippoRAG's graph retrieval?
items.object: Combining semantic document retrieval with HippoRAG
items.answer: Our naive, very basic solution for this is to use ensembling. You have a simple RAG framework where you get the top documents based on your query using context and semantic embeddings, and then you have HippoRAG on the other side. You can normalize the scores and combine or average them to obtain signal from both frameworks. That's the naive, basic idea. Adding the nodes to your graph is something we thought about, and after working with PPR a lot and getting a feel for what works and what doesn't, that will add a lot of density to the graph and make it much harder to do any sort of relevant traversal from it. One node will be connected to all the entities that happen in that node, so if you give that node any probability, the probability distribution will start being too spread out and won't work too well.

items.question: How do you assess the ability of long-context language models to consolidate knowledge beyond tasks like summarizing a large email history?
items.object: Long-context language models for multihop reasoning and knowledge consolidation
items.answer:
I think it's very interesting how good these models are at synthesizing stuff from long context. Honestly I've seen this myself, they can detect relevant things within that very long context and use it effectively. But I'm not super confident in their ability to get things that are not directly relevant to what they're looking at, but only relevant because they did some extra processing in some area of the long context. Basically, multihop reasoning within the prompt is still somewhat of a challenge.

It's currently under review, but I was working on this project that used long-context LMs for retrieval, basically answering the question: can we just use long-context LMs for this multihop question-answering setting? They are better than just embedding each thing separately. Compared to RAG, RAG just can't do multihop, but if you add these long-context LMs they'll be able to do multihop to some extent, and we actually see that in the attention patterns. It's not perfect, and as length increases, visibility drops. I don't know how much of this multihop process was happening in your 250,000 documents. I think if you look at the summary it created, you'd probably be able to link each point it produced one-to-one to some passage in your long context. They might even be doing some aggregation and summarization of multiple passages on multiple emails, but I'm not sure you're going to find extremely good consolidation of knowledge. That's the barrier I see with these long-context models, or where they could improve.

In recent work with Gemini 1.5, or the models we were using—we didn't get to one million tokens, but we were doing 40 or 80 passages even with GPT-4—so it's somewhat long context. Even in medium context this is a problem. In very long context I think it'll still be a problem. That's my assumption. I haven't actually tried it with Gemini.

items.question: How would you use long-context language models to search a knowledge graph if you could spend a quarter per query?
items.object: Long-context language models for knowledge-graph entry and traversal
items.answer: Yeah, if you can pay a quarter per query, an LM could do the graph entry probably very well. If we extract thousands or tens of thousands of entities of potential nodes to enter through, or even facts—I think facts might be better in this scenario—you get a bunch of facts from the knowledge graph that you created, and then you have your query. Long-context LMs are clearly going to be good at finding the relevant fact within this huge pile of facts, even in a huge knowledge base, even if you built it on the entire internet. I don't think you'll find enough relevant facts to your query that you won't find it in the top 10,000, for example. If you have 10,000 facts, you can use Gemini to find the entry point to the graph very well. Then you're probably going to do graph traversal with the LLM fairly well too, if you don't care about cost that much.

items.question: How do you think long-context language models and document consolidation should fit into a HippoRAG system without tight resource constraints?
items.object: Combining HippoRAG with long-context language models and document consolidation
items.answer: I think it is interesting to think about how to combine preprocessing your corpus with the power of long-context LMs and LMs in general to do self-correction, maintenance, and augmentation of this knowledge graph as you go. You also need a lot of that. RAPTOR, MemWalker, GraphRAG all do some sort of summarization of nodes, and I think that's probably important in a no-bounds HippoRAG setting. I would definitely combine all sorts of ideas from those papers, or basically this summarization or consolidation of documents based on some clustering. Obviously it has a role to play; it's just about how exactly, how big that role has to be, and how far can we go without it is also an interesting question.

items.question: How do you think HippoRAG should handle knowledge that is implicit in its recorded facts?
items.object: HippoRAG's handling of implicit knowledge
items.answer: One of Hippo's limitations is that it only deals with explicit knowledge. For example, you record that Cinderella lives happily ever after, but you don't record explicitly that the ending to the story is happy. That's something that you reflect on and say, okay, yeah, this is a happy ending. I think Hippo would definitely need some sort of process: let's look at the graph that we created, expand some nodes, create more relations, maybe delete relations that seem unnecessary, cluster happy-ending stories together, make nodes about the ending of a story. All sorts of interesting post-processing or maintenance of the graph that could be done automatically with LMs would be really interesting.

items.question: What do you find valuable about GTE from Contextual AI as an embedding model?
items.object: GTE from Contextual AI and instruction-tuned retrieval
items.answer: If you want higher performance and you're willing to pay a little more, there are some other embedding models. I was pretty happy with GTE from Contextual AI. items.question: How do you think about the tradeoff between using small chunks in HippoRAG and consolidating documents without chunking in LongRAG?
items.object: The tradeoff between small chunks in HippoRAG and knowledge consolidation without chunking in LongRAG
items.answer: I think it kind of becomes maybe a little bit too complex, and I would advocate for chunking with at least the current version of HippoRAG and current LMs, just a few sentences, a paragraph maybe, and then hierarchically summarize longer passages. It's a really interesting question because there's current work called LongRAG that says, okay, let's just do knowledge consolidation through no chunking. You have all the semantically similar documents, put them together, and use an LM encoder to embed those huge documents. That's how they solve this knowledge consolidation problem. I think it's an interesting idea, but in order to do better, the smaller the text snippets, the better attention you could place on different chunks. I think there's a tradeoff between a system like LongRAG and a system like HippoRAG, where you can have very small chunks but then consolidate them or connect ideas between them via preprocessing. For now, it's just two to three sentences.

items.question: What do you see as the biggest competency gap in language models apart from world knowledge?
items.object: Formal logic as a competency gap in language models
items.answer: There's a fun paper from some people from MIT, like Nancy Kanwisher or Aina Puce, that talks about how LMs are really good at formal linguistic competency. They're very good at phonology, syntax, local semantics. But then when it comes to—well, specifically, world knowledge is what we're talking about with continual learning—but also formal logic and social reasoning. I think the biggest competency gap apart from world knowledge that I see is formal logic. The bias toward system-one reasoning, fast heuristic-based reasoning, instead of more restrained, restrictive, constrained reasoning is a huge problem for us.

items.question: Why do you see modular architectures as a promising path toward better formal reasoning in language models?
items.object: Modular architectures for improving formal reasoning in language models
items.answer: In the same paper they talk about how this problem seems to be resolved through modularity in the brain. You definitely have a language circuit that's mostly doing, or probably doing, a lot of the system-one language-based reasoning, and then you have a bunch of other modules, and one of them is more responsible for system-two reasoning. I think there's also the school of thought that world-knowledge and formal-logic competencies are just going to rise from scale. I think this is possible but not guaranteed. Adding some sort of inductive priors of modularity, so you have different parts of the system that are architecturally different and learn different things, could actually accelerate the learning of more formal logic. That idea is really exciting to me research-wise. Obviously, it's not quite clear how the architectures have to look, but the idea that we need different architectures for different parts and learning to happen using these architectures is probably the best path forward, in my opinion.
